---
title: "Using ggmtools with other methods"
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
```

ggmtools has two layers:

* **Generics** (`pip_table()`, `pcor_estimate()`) that a package
  implements for its own fitted objects. spikeyglass and multiGGM provide
  methods, so the same downstream code runs on fits from either.
* **Matrix-level functions** for everything else: evaluation, losses,
  tuning, edge selection and edge tables. These take precision,
  partial-correlation, score or adjacency matrices, or vectors of
  probabilities and p-values, never a fitted object. They work with any
  estimator once its output is pulled out as a matrix.

This article shows the second layer with the joint graphical lasso (JGL;
Danaher, Wang & Witten 2014), then how to give a new method the first
layer.

## Which functions apply to which output

| The method returns | Examples | ggmtools functions |
|---|---|---|
| Precision matrices, one per group | JGL (fused or group), graphical lasso per group, spikeyglass, inverse covariance | `precision_to_pcor()`, `threshold_to_adjacency()`, `kl_divergence()`, `relative_frobenius()`, `ggm_bic()` (tuning), then everything below |
| Partial correlations, as matrices or upper-triangle vectors | multiGGM `pcor_estimate()`, DiNGO | `upper_tri_to_matrix()`, `diff_edge_table()`, `threshold_to_adjacency()` |
| Edge scores (higher = more likely an edge or a difference) | \|partial correlation\|, random-forest importance (JRF), D-trace \|Δ\|, test statistics | `roc_auc()`, `pr_auc()`, `confusion_at_threshold()`, `topk_overlap()` |
| Posterior edge probabilities | multiGGM (MRF priors and mGHS), spikeyglass `pip_table()` | `bayes_fdr()`, and the score functions above |
| Permutation or bootstrap null scores | any method refitted on permuted labels | `pooled_perm_pvalues()` |
| Estimated graphs (0/1) | any thresholded or selected graph | `confusion_at_threshold()`, `diff_adjacency()` |

## Example: the joint graphical lasso

The [JGL](https://cran.r-project.org/package=JGL) package returns a
list whose `theta` element holds one precision matrix per group. Tune the
two penalties with `ggm_bic()`, the BIC used with JGL in the Koyejo lab
code (smaller is better):

```{r jgl-tune, message = FALSE}
library(ggmtools)
library(JGL)

grid <- expand.grid(lambda1 = c(0.05, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3),
                    lambda2 = c(0.01, 0.05, 0.1))
grid$bic <- apply(grid, 1, function(g) {
  fit <- JGL(brca_pi3k, penalty = "fused", lambda1 = g[["lambda1"]],
             lambda2 = g[["lambda2"]], return.whole.theta = TRUE)
  ggm_bic(brca_pi3k, fit$theta)
})
best <- grid[which.min(grid$bic), ]
best
```

Refit at the chosen penalties and convert to partial correlations:

```{r jgl-fit}
fit <- JGL(brca_pi3k, penalty = "fused", lambda1 = best$lambda1,
           lambda2 = best$lambda2, return.whole.theta = TRUE)
genes <- colnames(brca_pi3k$Normal)
pcor <- lapply(fit$theta, precision_to_pcor)
names(pcor) <- names(brca_pi3k)

# Number of edges in each group's graph
sapply(fit$theta, function(theta) sum(threshold_to_adjacency(theta, 1e-8)) / 2)
```

The fused penalty sets many differences to exactly 0. `diff_edge_table()`
lists the rest in the shared edge-table format:

```{r jgl-diff}
d <- diff_edge_table(pcor$Normal, pcor$Tumor, threshold = 1e-8, varnames = genes)
nrow(d)
head(d[order(-abs(d$diff)), ])
```

Do JGL and the unregularized estimate agree on which edges change most?
JGL ties every edge it fuses at a difference of exactly 0, so
`topk_overlap()` counts those ties fairly instead of by edge position:

```{r jgl-overlap}
pcor_inv <- lapply(brca_pi3k, function(x) precision_to_pcor(solve(cov(x))))
k <- c(10, 25, 50, 100, 200)
data.frame(k = k,
           overlap = topk_overlap(abs(pcor$Normal - pcor$Tumor),
                                  abs(pcor_inv$Normal - pcor_inv$Tumor), k))
```

In a simulation, where the true graphs are known, the same estimates go
straight into `roc_auc()`, `pr_auc()` and `confusion_at_threshold()`, with
`abs(pcor$Normal)` (or `threshold_to_adjacency(fit$theta[[1]], 1e-8)`) as
the score and the true adjacency matrix as the truth.

## Example: the multiple graphical horseshoe (mGHS)

mGHS (Busatto & Stingo 2025) is fitted in multiGGM with
`multiggm_mcmc(method = "mghs")`. The fit is a multiGGM fit, so the
ggmtools generics work directly. The horseshoe prior has no point mass at
zero, so multiGGM defines the edge probability from the shrinkage weights,
\(P(w_{k,ij} > 0.5)\) with \(w = \lambda^2 / (1 + \lambda^2)\); see the
multiGGM documentation.

```{r mghs, eval = FALSE}
library(multiGGM)
fit <- multiggm_mcmc(data_list = brca_pi3k, method = "mghs")

pips <- pip_table(fit)       # long table: i, j, node1, node2, group, pip
pcor <- pcor_estimate(fit)   # list of partial-correlation matrices

normal <- pips[pips$group == "Normal", ]
normal$selected <- bayes_fdr(normal$pip, alpha = 0.05)
```

## Giving a new method the generics

`pip_table()` and `pcor_estimate()` form a common interface. Supporting a
new method means writing an *adapter*: S3 methods that convert its fitted
object into the shared output. For a JGL fit, which has class `"jgl"`:

```{r adapter}
pcor_estimate.jgl <- function(fit, varnames = NULL, groupnames = NULL, ...) {
  out <- lapply(fit$theta, precision_to_pcor)
  if (!is.null(varnames)) out <- lapply(out, function(m) {
    dimnames(m) <- list(varnames, varnames); m
  })
  names(out) <- groupnames %||% paste0("Group_", seq_along(out))
  out
}
`%||%` <- function(x, y) if (is.null(x)) y else x

str(pcor_estimate(fit, varnames = genes, groupnames = names(brca_pi3k)),
    max.level = 1)
```

In a script, defining the function is enough for dispatch. In a package,
register it with `S3method(ggmtools::pcor_estimate, jgl)` in the
NAMESPACE (with roxygen: `@exportS3Method ggmtools::pcor_estimate`). A
method that returns posterior probabilities can build its
`pip_table()` output with `as_pip_table()`.

## References

* Busatto, C. & Stingo, F.C. (2025). Inference of multiple
  high-dimensional networks with the Graphical Horseshoe prior. *Journal
  of Computational and Graphical Statistics*.
  [doi:10.1080/10618600.2024.2435480](https://doi.org/10.1080/10618600.2024.2435480)
* Danaher, P., Wang, P. & Witten, D.M. (2014). The joint graphical lasso
  for inverse covariance estimation across multiple classes. *Journal of
  the Royal Statistical Society: Series B*, 76(2), 373-397.
